questions.q: What is SQL Server Agent, fundamentally?
options: A service that runs alongside the database engine to execute scheduled work (jobs) and notify someone if that work fails — nothing more exotic than a built-in job scheduler
A general-purpose monitoring dashboard for the entire server
A tool that automatically rewrites poorly performing queries
A backup utility that runs independently of jobs or schedules
questions.explain: Agent's entire purpose is scheduling and running jobs, then reporting success or failure — not general monitoring or query tuning.

questions.q: How do a job, a job step, and a schedule relate to each other in SQL Server Agent?
options: A job is a container made of one or more steps (each a unit of work like T-SQL or PowerShell); a schedule is attached to the job as a whole, not to individual steps
A schedule contains multiple jobs, and each job has exactly one step
A step contains multiple jobs, each with its own schedule
Jobs, steps, and schedules are all independent objects with no relationship to each other
questions.explain: The job is the top-level container; steps run in sequence inside it; the schedule triggers the whole job, not a single step.

questions.q: What does SQL Server Agent's job history record, and why does it matter?
options: It automatically records every job run per step, including success/failure and duration — it's the first place to look when a job didn't do what it was supposed to
It only records jobs that failed, never successful runs
It must be manually enabled and configured before any history is recorded
It records only the job's schedule, not its actual execution results
questions.explain: Job history is automatic and per-step, making it the natural starting point for troubleshooting, covered fully in Lesson 62.

questions.q: Why does Azure SQL Database not support traditional SQL Server Agent, while SQL Server on an Azure VM and Managed Instance do?
options: Agent is fundamentally an instance-level service, and Azure SQL Database has no instance-level surface at all as a single-database PaaS product; Managed Instance and the VM both retain instance-level surface, so Agent works there
Microsoft simply forgot to implement Agent on Azure SQL Database and plans to add it later
Azure SQL Database is technically IaaS, which is incompatible with Agent
SQL Server Agent was deprecated on all Azure platforms in favor of Elastic Database Jobs
questions.explain: This is the same 'instance surface' concept from earlier in the course — Azure SQL Database trades away instance-level surface for its simpler model, losing Agent as part of that trade.

questions.q: If a DBA is asked to 'set up an Agent job' on Azure SQL Database, what is the accurate response according to this lesson?
options: That traditional SQL Server Agent isn't available on Azure SQL Database, and the actual equivalent is Elastic Database Jobs (or an external scheduler like Azure Automation)
Agent jobs work identically on Azure SQL Database, so proceed exactly as you would on-prem
It's impossible to schedule any automated work at all on Azure SQL Database
Azure SQL Database silently converts Agent job syntax into Managed Instance syntax automatically
questions.explain: Knowing the real platform boundary — and the real alternative — is the distinction the lesson highlights as genuinely testable and practically important.
